idiom_name: typed handler registry + discriminated-union dispatch over the event loop (worker_threads pool for parallel performers)
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the JavaScript runtime, so the event loop still performs the hand-off and the classic role structure is replaced by a Map or switch from message kind to handler: model messages as a discriminated union, dispatch on the discriminant, and let exhaustiveness checking (a never-returning default) make the compiler reject an unhandled message kind - a typed dispatcher with no runtime machinery. Handlers may be sync or async; the loop still runs them one at a time, so parallel performers require node:worker_threads behind typed postMessage wrappers, and the pool bookkeeping is the only part that resembles the classic structure. Reserve a real dispatcher class for policy decisions the compiler cannot express: least-busy selection, per-key ordering, rate limits.
pitfalls: A Map<string, Handler> loses the narrowing: the handler receives the union narrowing-free and needs a cast, which is where unsound dispatches survive the compiler; the switch plus never-check keeps type safety.
Message types are erased at runtime, so dispatch decisions still need validation at the boundary (zod/valibot or manual checks) - a cast on untrusted JSON is a latent crash.
Async handlers do not run in parallel in one JavaScript process: dispatch returns immediately but the handler body interleaves on the same loop, so CPU-heavy performers need worker_threads.
Fire-and-forget dispatch (no await, no catch) turns a rejected handler into an unhandled rejection and the message is lost with no trace.
Structured clone through worker_threads drops prototypes and functions, so class-based messages arrive as plain objects - pass plain data or rehydrate explicitly.
